::: {.cite-bar .domain-aid-sanctions}
[In force]{.status .status-in-force} [22 U.S.C. 2378d; 10 U.S.C. 362]{.cite}
:::

Two parallel provisions that bar U.S. assistance to any unit of a foreign security force when there is credible information that the unit committed a gross violation of human rights. They began as an appropriations rider sponsored by Senator Patrick Leahy.

## Key provisions

- 22 U.S.C. 2378d: no assistance under the Foreign Assistance Act or Arms Export Control Act to a tainted unit.
- 10 U.S.C. 362: no Defense Department training, equipment, or other assistance to a tainted unit.
- Assistance can resume if the foreign government is taking effective steps to bring those responsible to justice.
- Requires a vetting process and, for the State Department law, notice to the foreign government.

## Why it matters

They operate at the level of the unit, which lets the United States keep working with a country while excluding specific battalions. They constrain assistance under the [Foreign Assistance Act](faa-1961.qmd), the [Arms Export Control Act](aeca-1976.qmd), and the Defense Department programs in [Chapter 16 of Title 10](seccoop-2016.qmd). Consistency of application across recipients is the usual criticism.

## Current status

In force. The State Department version is Section 620M of the Foreign Assistance Act; the Defense Department version was made permanent in Title 10 in 2014.

## Connections
